title: Fix applyInPandasWithState failure with PyArrow 26 due to float slice offsets
description:
PyArrow 26.0.0 made {{RecordBatch.slice}} validate {{offset}}/{{length}} with {{operator.index}} (previously a float was silently truncated by the Cython int64 conversion).

In {{ApplyInPandasWithStateSerializer.load_stream}}, {{startOffset}}/{{numRows}} are read from the state struct column converted to pandas. When an Arrow batch contains null padding rows ({{ApplyInPandasWithStateWriter.EMPTY_STATE_METADATA_ROW}}, i.e. whenever a group has more than one data row), the int32 fields of the struct are promoted to float64 by the pandas conversion, so {{data_batch.slice(data_start_offset, num_data_rows)}} fails with:

{noformat}
TypeError: 'float' object cannot be interpreted as an integer
{noformat}

This breaks {{applyInPandasWithState}} for users on PyArrow 26, and {{FlatMapGroupsInPandasWithStateSuite}} in the branch-4.0 / branch-4.1 scheduled builds since PyArrow 26.0.0 was released (the JVM build job installs an unpinned pyarrow).

branch-4.2 and later are not affected: SPARK-54962 converts nullable integers with {{integer_object_nulls=True}}, so the values stay ints.

title: Avoid per-character synchronized reads in the bounded event log line reader
description:
SPARK-59407 replaced {{Source.getLines()}} in {{ReplayListenerBus.replay(InputStream, ...)}} with a bounded line reader so that over-long event log lines are skipped instead of materialized (SPARK-59804 later fixed its byte accounting). The reader calls {{BufferedReader.read()}} once per character, and {{BufferedReader.read()}} takes a lock on every call, so splitting lines is several times slower than the previous {{readLine()}}-based reading. In the review of SPARK-59804 (https://github.com/apache/spark/pull/59074), line splitting was measured at about 14x slower.

This slows down every replay through the {{InputStream}} overload: loading application UIs in the History Server, event log compaction, and listing with fast in-progress parsing. SPARK-60109 also routes the History Server end-event reparse through this reader. For compressed logs, that reparse reads most of the decompressed file, because the skip target is computed from the compressed length, so it makes the listing of completed applications slower as well. In a local measurement of that reparse path (210 MB of uncompressed event lines, lz4 and zstd), it took about 0.17 s with {{Source.getLines()}} and 0.9-1.05 s with the bounded reader.

Proposed fix: read decoded characters in bulk (e.g. into a {{char[]}} buffer) and scan for '\n' there, instead of calling {{read()}} per character. Keep the current semantics: the UTF-8 content byte limit with the trailing-CR allowance, physical line indices including skipped lines, strict decoding, and releasing the buffer of an over-long line while it is drained. A prototype of the bulk scan brought the reparse path above back to about 0.17 s.

title: CrossValidatorModel.load() returns the last fold's sub-models for every fold
description:
When a CrossValidatorModel is saved with sub-models and loaded back in PySpark, every fold's entry of \{{subModels}} refers to the same list, which holds the last fold's models.

The cause is in \{{CrossValidatorModelReader.load}} (python/pyspark/ml/tuning.py):
{code:python}
subModels = [[None] * len(estimatorParamMaps)] * numFolds
{code}
{\{[x] * n}} repeats a reference to the same inner list, so each fold's assignment overwrites the previous one. \{{CrossValidator._fit}}, \{{CrossValidatorModel.copy}} and \{{_from_java}} all build an independent list per fold, as does the Scala reader (\{{Array.fill(numFolds)(...)}}).

The files on disk are correct. Only the PySpark reader is affected. \{{bestModel}} and \{{avgMetrics}} are not affected. However, saving a loaded model again writes the last fold's models into every fold directory, so the original sub-models are lost.

*Reproduce*
{code:python}
from pyspark.ml.classification import LogisticRegression
from pyspark.ml.evaluation import BinaryClassificationEvaluator
from pyspark.ml.linalg import Vectors
from pyspark.ml.tuning import CrossValidator, CrossValidatorModel, ParamGridBuilder

df = spark.createDataFrame(
    [(Vectors.dense([float(i)]), float(i % 2)) for i in range(30)], ["features", "label"])
lr = LogisticRegression(maxIter=2)
grid = ParamGridBuilder().addGrid(lr.regParam, [0.0, 0.1]).build()
cv = CrossValidator(estimator=lr, estimatorParamMaps=grid,
                    evaluator=BinaryClassificationEvaluator(),
                    numFolds=3, collectSubModels=True, seed=1)
model = cv.fit(df)
model.write().save("/tmp/cv")
loaded = CrossValidatorModel.load("/tmp/cv")

print([m.coefficients for m in model.subModels[0]])   # fold 0
print([m.coefficients for m in loaded.subModels[0]])  # same as fold 2
print(loaded.subModels[0] is loaded.subModels[1])     # True
{code}

First coefficient of each sub-model:
|| ||fold0||fold1||fold2||
|after fit|[0.0705, 0.0439]|[0.0067, 0.0047]|[-0.0155, -0.0108]|
|on disk after save|[0.0705, 0.0439]|[0.0067, 0.0047]|[-0.0155, -0.0108]|
|after load|[-0.0155, -0.0108]|[-0.0155, -0.0108]|[-0.0155, -0.0108]|

The existing test in python/pyspark/ml/tests/test_tuning.py does not catch this. It compares \{{model.subModels[i][j].uid}} with itself, and after loading it only checks the list lengths. All sub-models share the estimator's uid, so a uid comparison would not detect it either.

The line was introduced by SPARK-33520.

title: Apply the replay line-length limit and UTF-8-safe line alignment to the History Server end-event reparse
description:
When building the application listing, FsHistoryProvider looks for the application end event by reopening the last event log file, skipping to {{len - spark.history.fs.endEventReparseChunkSize}} bytes, wrapping the stream in {{Source.fromInputStream(in)(Codec.UTF8).getLines()}}, dropping the first (partial) line with {{source.next()}}, and replaying the rest through {{ReplayListenerBus.replay(Iterator[String], ...)}}. With the defaults (completed apps, 1m chunk), every completed application takes this path, and because the target is computed from the compressed length while the skip runs on the decompressed stream, most of a compressed log can be read there.

This path has three problems:

1. The Iterator overload bypasses the bounded line reader added by SPARK-59407 / SPARK-59804, so {{spark.history.fs.eventLog.maxLineLength}} does not apply and an over-long line is fully materialized.
2. If the skip target lands inside a multi-byte UTF-8 character (e.g. CJK SQL text or job descriptions, which Jackson writes as raw UTF-8), {{source.next()}} throws {{MalformedInputException}} before replay starts. mergeApplicationListing only logs the error, and since the placeholder listing entry was already written with the same file size, the log is never retried, so the completed application stays missing from the listing (the target is deterministic, so restarting the History Server fails the same way).
3. Line numbers in the replay diagnostics (JSON parse errors, "Malformed line #N", the truncation warning and the over-long line warning) are relative to the skip point but are printed next to the full file path, which makes them misleading.

Proposed fix: after skipping, discard the partial first line at the raw byte level (0x0A never occurs inside a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence) before any decoding, then replay through the InputStream overload so the line-length limit and strict decoding apply, and label the source name with the byte offset that line numbers are counted from.

This is the tail-reparse follow-up discussed in https://github.com/apache/spark/pull/59074.

title: PlanMerger loses a reused filter attribute that an earlier merge folded into another filter
ForSt: rescale restore never closes the temporary DB's DBOptions copy, leaking the slot-shared block cache
description:
h3. Problem

{{ForStIncrementalRestoreOperation#restoreTempDBInstance}} opens every temporary restore DB with a native copy of the backend's DB options, and nothing ever closes it:

{code:java}
// do not relocate log file for temp db
DBOptions dbOptions = new DBOptions(this.forstHandle.getDbOptions());
dbOptions.setDbLogDir("");
RocksDB restoreDb = ForStOperationUtils.openDB(..., dbOptions);
return new RestoredDBInstance(restoreDb, ...); // dbOptions is not passed on and not closed
{code}

{{RestoredDBInstance#close()}} closes the DB, its column family handles/options and its {{ReadOptions}}, but not this {{DBOptions}}.

With managed memory ({{state.backend.forst.memory.managed: true}}, the default), the copied native {{DBOptions}} shares the slot's {{WriteBufferManager}} (a {{shared_ptr}} in the C++ {{DBOptions}}), and the WBM holds the slot-shared block cache, because memtable memory is charged to the cache. When the backend is later disposed, all Java handles ({{RocksDB}}, {{LRUCache}}, {{WriteBufferManager}}, {{DBOptions}}) are closed, but the leaked copy keeps the native WBM, and through it the whole block cache with its cached blocks, alive until the TaskManager JVM exits.

Temporary DBs are used for multi-handle restores (every scale-in and some scale-outs), so each such restore pins the block cache of the new backend. That memory leaks at the next restart on the same TaskManager: rescale, failover, or an in-place restart by the adaptive scheduler or autoscaler. Each leak is up to one slot's block cache capacity. A few rescales or restart attempts on a long-lived TM can OOM-kill the container.

* Not affected: unmanaged ForSt memory (no WBM, the copy pins only a few KB), same-parallelism failovers (single-handle restore, no temp DB), and the RocksDB backend ({{RocksDBIncrementalRestoreOperation}} does not copy the options).

h3. Evidence

*Production* (ForSt + async state V2, Flink 2.3.0, one TM with 3 slots and ~0.5 GB block cache per slot, job restarted in place via {{PUT /jobs/<id>/resource-requirements}}). "Unexplained native" = native anon RSS outside the heap, minus the live ForSt {{block-cache-usage}} and memtables:

||Restart||Backends disposed||Their cache when disposed||Unexplained native||Step||
|baseline p=1|-|-|3,130 MiB| |
|p=1 → 3|1 (restored by a scale-in)|full, ~420 MiB|3,576 MiB|*+446*|
|p=3 → 1|3|young, ~100–200 MiB|3,604 MiB|+28|
|p=1 → 3|1 (restored by a scale-in)|full, ~413 MiB|4,040 MiB|*+436*|
|p=3 → 1|3|young, ~100–200 MiB|4,087 MiB|+47|

* jemalloc stats on the live TM: the retained memory is live allocations, not pages kept by the allocator (allocated 2.76 GiB, resident 3.16 GiB, dirty 34 MiB).
* A heap dump shows that every Java-side object of the disposed backends is closed ({{owningHandle_ = false}}), so the memory is held from the native side.
* With {{state.backend.forst.memory.managed: false}} (private caches, no WBM), the same restart freed all of the disposed backends' ForSt memory (+1 MiB).

*JNI-only reproduction* (forstjni 0.1.8, jemalloc with {{dirty_decay_ms:0,muzzy_decay_ms:0}}): a shared {{LRUCache}} + {{WriteBufferManager(cache)}} + {{DBOptions}} with the WBM, cache filled to ~308 MiB, then everything closed. Retained RSS: 94 MiB with no copy, *422 MiB with an unclosed {{new DBOptions(options)}} copy*, 90 MiB when the copy is closed too.

*MiniCluster reproduction* (attached {{ScaleInLeakCheck.java}}): a ForSt async-state job with 400k keys, a 2-slot TM with 1 GB managed memory, restored alternately at p=2 and p=1 from native savepoints in one JVM. RSS after each run's MiniCluster has shut down, stock flink-dist 2.3.0 vs. the same with the fix:

||Run||Stock RSS||Step||Fixed RSS||Step||
|base|2,150 MiB||2,150 MiB||
|0: p=2, fresh|2,307 MiB|+157|2,308 MiB|+158|
|1: p=1 (scale-in)|2,713 MiB|*+406*|2,354 MiB|+46|
|2: p=2|2,759 MiB|+46|2,403 MiB|+49|
|3: p=1 (scale-in)|3,182 MiB|*+423*|2,441 MiB|+38|
|4: p=2|3,214 MiB|+32|2,468 MiB|+27|
|5: p=1 (scale-in)|3,632 MiB|*+418*|2,504 MiB|+36|
|total|| *+1,482 MiB* || +354 MiB|

Stock leaks about one slot's block cache (~410 MiB) on every scale-in. With the fix, every run adds 27–49 MiB regardless of direction, with no scale-in pattern (JVM and allocator warm-up). Run with {{-Xms2g -Xmx2g -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch}} and {{LD_PRELOAD=libjemalloc.so.2 MALLOC_CONF=dirty_decay_ms:0,muzzy_decay_ms:0}}, so that RSS reflects live native allocations.

h3. Proposed fix

Pass the copy to {{RestoredDBInstance}}, close it in {{close()}} right after the DB, and close it in {{restoreTempDBInstance}} if {{openDB}} fails. The copy is created per temporary DB and used only to open it, so closing it drops only this copy's references and doesn't affect the main DB's options, WBM or cache. PR to follow.

We are deploying this patch to production on top of 2.3.0.

title: Use identity equality for HybridRowQueue
description:
HybridRowQueue is a case class, so two queues created in the same task with the same TaskMemoryManager, temp dir, number of fields, SerializerManager and lockFree flag are equal. Because HybridRowQueue is a MemoryConsumer (via HybridQueue), this breaks memory management:

1. TaskMemoryManager tracks consumers in a HashSet. A second queue that equals an already registered one is never added, so it is never offered for spilling when another consumer needs memory, and its memory is not attributed in the memory usage breakdown on OOM.
2. HybridQueue.spill(size, trigger) returns 0 when trigger == this, which uses equals. A queue therefore refuses to spill when an equal but distinct queue triggers the spill.

This can happen in a real query, e.g. when several partitions evaluated by a Python UDF node are processed in one task (coalesce), or when both sides of a sort-merge join contain Python UDF eval nodes with the same input width.

The fix is to give HybridRowQueue identity equality by making it a regular class.

title: HTTP lookup source drops the row for a failed call with continue-on-error unless the planner calls applyReadableMetadata
description:
With \{{http.source.lookup.continue-on-error}} = true, the docs state that a failed lookup call completes the join "without content in the expected enrichment columns", i.e. the enrichment columns are null. For a table without metadata columns this only holds if the planner happened to call \{{SupportsReadingMetadata#applyReadableMetadata}}:

{code:sql}
CREATE TABLE http_lookup (id STRING, name STRING, age INT) WITH (
  'connector' = 'rest-lookup',
  'url' = '...',
  'format' = 'json',
  'http.source.lookup.continue-on-error' = 'true');

-- the endpoint returns an error for the key
SELECT o.id, l.name FROM orders AS o
JOIN http_lookup FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF o.proc_time AS l ON o.id = l.id;
{code}

* If a projection is pushed into the lookup source (as in this query), the planner records an empty ReadingMetadata ability, \{{applyReadableMetadata([], ...)}} sets \{{producedDataType}}, and the failed call yields a row with null enrichment columns.
* If no projection is pushed (the query uses all columns), \{{producedDataType}} stays null and \{{HttpTableLookupFunction}} returns no row ("return the same way as ignore", HttpTableLookupFunction.java:174), so the inner lookup join drops the row.

{\{HttpLookupTableSource}} sets \{{producedDataType}} only in \{{applyReadableMetadata}} (HttpLookupTableSource.java:339); the constructor and \{{applyProjection}} leave it unset, and \{{copy()}} does not carry it or \{{metadataKeys}} over. The lookup function uses it to size the output row when the response has no data.

FLINK-38569 stops the planner from recording the empty ReadingMetadata ability, which would make the second behavior apply to all queries against tables without metadata columns.

title: LikeSimplification duplicates a nondeterministic input of a single-pattern LIKE
description:
For a LIKE with a single pattern of the form 'prefix%suffix', LikeSimplification rewrites `input LIKE pattern` into `OctetLength(input) >= n AND StartsWith(input, prefix) AND EndsWith(input, suffix)`, copying `input` three times without checking that it is deterministic. A nondeterministic input is then evaluated once per copy, so the predicate can be true for a row where no single value matches. The LikeAll/LikeAny cases already guard with CollapseProject.isCheap.

Example: with a nondeterministic UDF `pick()` that returns 'ay' or 'bz' at random, `SELECT pick() LIKE 'a%z' AS r FROM range(0, 1000, 1, 1)` returned 256 true rows in one run, where the correct count is 0.

Raised in https://github.com/apache/spark/pull/59209#discussion_r4199845624

title: Table API row() fails when AS aliases produce duplicate field names
description:
FLINK-39253 names the fields of the Table API \{{row()}} function after the \{{AS}} aliases of its arguments. An argument without an alias still gets \{{f<index>}}. The names are not de-duplicated, so the call fails when two of them collide:

{code:java}
row($("a").as("f1"), $("b"))         // f1, f1
row($("a").as("x"), $("b").as("x"))  // x, x
row($("a"), $("b").as("f0"))         // f0, f0
{code}

Each fails during resolution with:
{noformat}
org.apache.flink.table.api.ValidationException: Invalid function call:
...
Caused by: org.apache.flink.table.api.ValidationException: Field names must be unique. Found duplicates: [f1]
{noformat}

Before FLINK-39253, all three calls resolved and named the fields f0 and f1. FLINK-39253 is only on master, so the regression would first ship in 2.4.0. SQL \{{ROW(...)}} is not affected.

Suggested fix: when the resolved names are not unique, fall back to \{{f<index>}} for every field. That keeps every call that resolved before FLINK-39253 working. A narrower option is to fall back only for the clashing field, but then a field's name depends on its neighbours.

title: Ensure Ivy contexts are popped after Maven resolution failures
description:
{{MavenUtils.resolveMavenCoordinatesWithCancellation}} creates a primary Ivy instance and may create a second no-cache Ivy instance for fallback resolution.

Both paths call {{{}Ivy.pushContext(){}}}, but the corresponding {{popContext()}} calls currently occur only on successful paths. Exceptions from resolve, retrieve, or cancellation can bypass cleanup and leave thread-local Ivy context state behind.

If the thread is reused, a later Maven resolution may observe stale Ivy state or settings.

h2. Proposed change

Pair every {{Ivy.pushContext()}} with {{popContext()}} in a {{finally}} block.

A small {{withIvyContext}} helper can wrap both the primary and no-cache resolution paths while preserving their nesting and fallback behavior.

h2. Acceptance criteria

  * Primary Ivy context is removed after success and failure.
  * No-cache fallback context is removed after success and failure.
  * Existing retry-without-cache behavior remains unchanged.
  * Add regression tests that inject failures into both paths and verify that the context is restored.
  * A subsequent Maven resolution on the same thread succeeds without inheriting stale context.

title: Avoid copying Ivy caches when cloning ArtifactManager
description:
SPARK-59553 added per-session Maven resolution to ArtifactManager. The resolver stores its Ivy cache at {{{}artifactPath/.ivy-cache{}}}. {{ArtifactManager.clone()}} recursively copies the entire parent {{{}artifactPath{}}}. After Maven resolution, this copies both:

  * The disposable Ivy cache, including downloaded and retrieved jars.
  * The installed session artifacts under {{{}jars/{}}}, {{{}classes/{}}}, and other artifact directories.

For a large transitive dependency tree, every initialized cloned session can therefore incur unnecessary disk usage and clone latency.
h2. Proposed change

Update {{ArtifactManager.clone()}} to exclude the top-level {{.ivy-cache}} directory while continuing to copy installed session artifacts.

The cloned session should lazily create a fresh {{.ivy-cache}} if it later performs Maven resolution.
h2. Acceptance criteria

  * Installed jars, classes, and Python artifacts remain available in the cloned session.
  * The parent's {{.ivy-cache}} is not copied.
  * Maven resolution in the cloned session still succeeds and creates a new cache when needed.
  * Add a regression test covering these behaviors.

Ensure token manager cleanup in testNodesLoadedAfterRestart
description:
TestZKDelegationTokenSecretManager.testNodesLoadedAfterRestart() destroys the original DelegationTokenManager before creating a replacement,
but does not destroy the replacement when the test finishes. Cleanup is also not guaranteed if initialization or an assertion fails.

The teardown then closes ZooKeeper while the ExpiredTokenRemover thread may still be running.
The thread can encounter ConnectionLossException while updating the shared key ID counter and call Runtime.exit(-1),
terminating the Surefire JVM with exit code 255.

TorchDistributor logs a TypeError instead of a warning when the log streaming server fails to start
description:
In \{{TorchDistributor._run_distributed_training}} (\{{python/pyspark/ml/torch/distributor.py}}), the warning emitted when the log streaming server fails to start has a stray comma, so the error message is passed to \{{logger.warning}} as a separate positional argument:

{code:python}
self.logger.warning(
    "Start torch distributor log streaming server failed, "
    "You cannot receive logs sent from distributor workers, ",   # <- stray comma
    f"error: \{repr(e)}.",
)
{code}

Since the message has no %-placeholder, \{{logging}} fails with "TypeError: not all arguments converted during string formatting" when the record is formatted. Training continues (the fallback added in SPARK-44909 still sets the port to -1), but instead of a one-line warning:

* with default logging settings the user sees a "--- Logging error ---" traceback that looks like a crash;
* with \{{logging.raiseExceptions = False}} the warning is dropped entirely, so the user never learns why worker logs are missing;
* \{{record.getMessage()}} raises, so the warning cannot be asserted in tests.

h3. Reproduction

Call \{{_run_distributed_training}} with \{{LogStreamingServer.start}} raising, e.g. \{{OSError("Address already in use")}}:

{noformat}
--- Logging error ---
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../logging/__init__.py", line 377, in getMessage
    msg = msg % self.args
TypeError: not all arguments converted during string formatting
Call stack:
  File ".../pyspark/ml/torch/distributor.py", line 815, in _run_distributed_training
    self.logger.warning(
Message: 'Start torch distributor log streaming server failed, You cannot receive logs sent from distributor workers, '
Arguments: ("error: OSError('Address already in use').",)
{noformat}

h3. Proposed fix

Make it a single format string with the exception passed as an argument:

{code:python}
self.logger.warning(
    "Start torch distributor log streaming server failed. "
    "You cannot receive logs sent from distributor workers, error: %r.",
    e,
)
{code}

plus a unit test that makes \{{LogStreamingServer.start}} fail and checks the warning message.

title: Fix BIN BY boundary index overflow
Handle all-null partial and final tuple/theta intersection aggregates
description:
{{{}tuple_intersection_agg_double{}}}, {{{}tuple_intersection_agg_integer{}}}, and {{theta_intersection_agg}} skip null sketch inputs. When a group or partial sees no non-null input, its intersection remains untouched. JVM partial serialization and final evaluation both call DataSketches {{getResult()}} on that state, which throws {{SketchesStateException}} ("getResult() with no intervening intersections is not a legal result"). Thus an all-null partial can fail before another partition's valid contribution is merged, and a fully all-null group throws instead of producing a valid empty sketch. A genuinely empty intersection after non-null input is a different, valid result.
h3. Expected behavior
 * Partial/PartialMerge preserves an explicit no-non-null-input state. Merge treats that state as no contribution on either side; returning a valid empty sketch from a partial would incorrectly erase another partition's non-empty contribution.

 * Final/Complete returns a valid empty sketch when the entire group had no non-null sketch inputs, for grouped and ungrouped aggregation, without throwing.

 * A valid empty input sketch remains a real contribution, and disjoint non-null sketches legitimately produce an empty intersection.

h3. Acceptance criteria
 * All-null grouped and ungrouped aggregates return a valid empty sketch (estimate 0), with no exception during Partial, PartialMerge, Final, or Complete.

 * A group split across partitions into an all-null partial and a non-empty partial produces the non-empty partial's result, in either merge order; other groups remain unaffected.

 * Valid empty input sketches, disjoint non-null intersections, and supported JVM/Photon mixed-stage execution keep their correct semantics.

title: Variant builder mishandles a nested variant and a value of exactly 16 MiB
Reject VARIANT where SQL needs equality. Byte comparison gives wrong results in GROUP BY, DISTINCT, joins and =
description:
h2. Problem

Flink compares VARIANT values by their binary encoding. One logical value has many encodings. Queries that group, deduplicate, join or compare on VARIANT therefore return wrong results, without any error.

{code:sql}
-- t(s STRING) has three rows:
--   row 1: \{"a":1,"b":2}
--   row 2: \{"b":2,"a":1}
--   row 3: \{"a":1,"c":3}
SELECT a, COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT PARSE_JSON(s)['a'] AS a FROM t) GROUP BY a;
{code}

{noformat}
Query                                                        Expected            Actual
GROUP BY PARSE_JSON(s)['a']                                  one group, count 3  three groups, count 1 each
COUNT(DISTINCT PARSE_JSON(s)) over row 1 and row 2           1                   2
WHERE PARSE_JSON(s)['a'] = PARSE_JSON('1')                   3 rows              0 rows
l JOIN r ON PARSE_JSON(l.s)['id'] = PARSE_JSON(r.s)['id']    1 row               0 rows
  with l = \{"id":7,"x":1} and r = \{"y":2,"id":7}
{noformat}

The actual results come from VariantSemanticTest on master 5afe863af62. Example output for the GROUP BY:
{noformat}
Expecting actual:
  ["+I[1, 1]", "+I[1, 1]", "+I[1, 1]"]
to contain exactly in any order:
  ["+I[1, 1]", "-U[1, 1]", "+U[1, 2]", "-U[1, 2]", "+U[1, 3]"]
{noformat}

h2. Cause

A VARIANT is two byte arrays. The metadata is a dictionary of key names. The value refers to keys by their position in that dictionary. Flink treats two VARIANTs as equal only if both arrays are byte-equal:
* Grouping, DISTINCT and join keys are BinaryRowData. \{{AbstractBinaryWriter#writeVariant}} writes the dictionary and the value bytes into the key, and BinaryRowData hashes and compares those bytes.
* \{{=}} calls \{{BinaryVariant#equals}}, which compares the value, the dictionary and the position.

One value has many valid encodings:
* The dictionary lists keys in the order they first appear. Row 1 and row 2 get different dictionaries.
* A field taken by field access keeps the full dictionary of its parent object. The number 1 from row 1 differs from the number 1 from row 3 and from PARSE_JSON('1').
* Numbers keep their storage width. PARSE_JSON('1') is a TINYINT, CAST(CAST(1 AS BIGINT) AS VARIANT) is a BIGINT, and PARSE_JSON('1.0') is a DECIMAL. All three print as 1.

The variant encoding spec allows all of these. For the same reason, the Iceberg spec defines no hash for variant.

h2. Proposal

Reject VARIANT where SQL needs equality, like ORDER BY on VARIANT is rejected today (\{{TypeCheckUtils#isComparable}}). Users cast to a concrete type first. That already works:
{code:sql}
SELECT a, COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT CAST(PARSE_JSON(s)['a'] AS INT) AS a FROM t) GROUP BY a;
-- one group, count 3
{code}

Reject VARIANT, also when nested in ROW, ARRAY or MAP, in:
* GROUP BY keys, including GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP, CUBE and window aggregations
* DISTINCT aggregates and SELECT DISTINCT
* equi-join keys
* =, <>, IN, IS DISTINCT FROM and IS NOT DISTINCT FROM between VARIANT operands
* UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT without ALL
* PARTITION BY of OVER windows, Top-N, deduplication, process table functions and MATCH_RECOGNIZE

Still allowed: VARIANT as an aggregate argument such as COUNT(v), FIRST_VALUE(v) and LAST_VALUE(v), IS NULL, IS NOT NULL, field access and casts.

The error should name the clause and suggest a cast, for example:
{noformat}
VARIANT cannot be used as a grouping key because VARIANT values have no equality. Cast the value to a concrete type first, for example CAST(v['a'] AS INT).
{noformat}

Open question: VARIANT as a MAP key. MAP lookups use the same byte equality.

h2. Other systems

||System||Behavior||
|Spark / Databricks|VARIANT is not comparable since SPARK-47569. GROUP BY fails with GROUP_EXPRESSION_TYPE_IS_NOT_ORDERABLE. DISTINCT and set operations fail. PARTITION BY fails with PARTITION_BY_VARIANT. Databricks docs: "The VARIANT data type cannot be used for comparisons, grouping, ordering, and set operations."|
|BigQuery|JSON is neither groupable nor comparable, and cannot be a partition or cluster key. Users extract with JSON_VALUE first.|
|Apache Iceberg|The spec defines no hash for variant, because equivalent values have several representations.|

Sources:
* https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/semi-structured/variant
* https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/master/sql/catalyst/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/catalyst/expressions/ExprUtils.scala (checkValidGroupingExprs)
* https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/master/sql/catalyst/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/catalyst/analysis/CheckAnalysis.scala (variantColumnInSetOperation, PARTITION_BY_VARIANT)
* https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/data-types
* https://github.com/apache/iceberg/blob/main/format/spec.md

h2. Compatibility

* Flink 2.1 to 2.3 accept these queries. After the change they fail at validation. This needs a release note.
* Existing tests assert the old behavior and must change: VariantSemanticTest VARIANT_AS_AGG_KEY, and the COUNT(DISTINCT v) in BUILTIN_AGG and BUILTIN_AGG_WITH_RETRACTION.
* Open question: a job restored from a compiled plan skips SQL validation. Should it fail too, or keep running?
* Supporting equality later stays compatible, because it only accepts more queries.

h2. Alternatives considered

* Write a field value with only the keys it uses. This fixes scalar fields, but not objects or number widths.
* A canonical encoding: sorted dictionary, no unused keys, smallest number width. This changes the bytes of existing state, and data from other writers still differs because the spec allows several encodings.
* Semantic equality and hashing on decoded values. Correct, but a larger design: how 1 compares to 1.0, NaN, and the timestamp kinds. It can follow later.

h2. Tests

Four VariantSemanticTest programs reproduce the bug and fail on master as shown above: variant-field-as-agg-key, variant-object-as-distinct-key, variant-field-equals-variant and variant-field-as-join-key. With the fix they become failing-SQL checks for the new error. A fifth program, variant-field-cast-as-agg-key, checks the CAST workaround and passes today.

title: Generated columns, DELETE and CHECK constraints break on NULLIF or BETWEEN over a non-cheap operand
LATERAL SNAPSHOT join wrongly rejected when a local filter targets the join key column
description:
A LATERAL SNAPSHOT join that has a valid equi-join predicate is wrongly rejected with

  "LATERAL SNAPSHOT join requires at least one equality predicate."

whenever the query also has a local filter on the same column that carries the
equi-join predicate.

Example (fails):

  SELECT o.order_id, c.city
  FROM orders AS o
  JOIN LATERAL SNAPSHOT(
    input => TABLE customers,
    on_time => DESCRIPTOR(rowtime)
  ) AS c
  ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
  WHERE o.customer_id = 3200;

A filter on any other (non-join-key) column, e.g. WHERE o.amount = 42, works fine.

Root cause:
LogicalJoinToLateralSnapshotJoinRule enforces the equi-key requirement via
join.analyzeCondition().leftKeys.isEmpty(). When the local filter targets the
join key, Calcite's constant propagation pushes o.customer_id = 3200 to the probe
side, infers customers.customer_id = 3200 on the build side, and then simplifies
the join condition o.customer_id = c.customer_id to TRUE. analyzeCondition() then
reports no equi-keys and the rule rejects a join that is in fact an equi-join. The
error message is also misleading, since an equality predicate was provided.

title: LATERAL SNAPSHOT build side passes TRY_RESOLVE with non-deterministic columns
Strip aliases from a DSv2 reported ordering on a nested field
description:
{{V2ScanPartitioningAndOrdering}} converts a scan's {{SupportsReportOrdering}} ordering on every application of the rule, and unlike the partitioning pass, the ordering pass has no guard. For a nested sort key such as {{s.x}}, {{LogicalPlan.resolve}} returns a new {{Alias(GetStructField(...))}} with a fresh {{ExprId}} each time.

As a result:
* In testing, the "Early Filter and Projection Push-Down" Once batch fails its idempotence check:
{noformat}
Once strategy's idempotence is broken for batch Early Filter and Projection Push-Down
{noformat}
* In production, the aliased {{SortOrder}} never semantically equals a required {{SortOrder}} on {{s.x}}, so Spark adds a redundant {{SortExec}} even though the scan reports that ordering.
* {{PlanMerger}} treats two derivations of the same nested ordering as different, so scan merging can decline.

Repro: a DSv2 scan that implements {{SupportsReportOrdering}} and reports {{sort(FieldReference(Seq("s", "x")), ASC, NULLS_FIRST)}} on a table with a struct column {{s}}, then a query such as {{SELECT s.x FROM t}} or {{sortWithinPartitions($"s.x")}}.

Proposed fix: strip aliases from the converted sort orders in the ordering pass (e.g. {{trimAliases}} from {{AliasHelper}}), so that repeated applications produce equal plans and the reported ordering can satisfy a required ordering.

This is pre-existing on master. It was found while reviewing SPARK-59721 (https://github.com/apache/spark/pull/58979). A related but separate issue: a nested partition key gets the same {{Alias}} and is rejected by {{KeyedPartitioning.supportsExpressions}}, so storage-partitioned join never applies to it.

title: Code splitter should generate same code after repeated runs
lag/lead return NULL and other window frames silently corrupt results for partitions larger than Int.MaxValue rows
description:
h2. Summary

{{org.apache.spark.sql.execution.ExternalAppendOnlyUnsafeRowArray}} counts the buffered rows
of a window partition in a 32-bit {{Int}} ({{numRows}}). When a single window partition exceeds
{{Int.MaxValue}} (2,147,483,647) rows, {{numRows}} overflows and wraps negative. Downstream
window-frame logic that reads this count (and the per-row index/bounds, also tracked as 32-bit
{{Int}}) then misbehaves, producing *silently wrong results* with no exception.

This is the read-path counterpart of the write/insertion-path overflow fixed by SPARK-51757,
which did not widen {{numRows}}/{{length}}.

h2. Symptom

For {{lag}}/{{lead}}, the offset frame ({{FrameLessOffsetWindowFunctionFrame}}) guards with
{{absOffset > rows.length}}. With a negative (wrapped) {{length}}, the guard misfires and the
frame emits the function's default value (NULL) for *every* row.

Confirmed reproduction (classic non-Photon {{WindowExec}}; ~30 min over 2.2B rows):

{code:sql}
SELECT count(*) AS n_rows, max(prev) AS max_prev, max(id) AS max_id
FROM (
  SELECT id, lag(id, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY CAST(0 AS INT) ORDER BY id) AS prev
  FROM range(2200000000)
);
{code}

Observed vs. correct:

{code}
n_rows   = 2200000000     (all rows funnel to ONE partition via PARTITION BY a constant)
max_prev = NULL           <-- BUG. Correct value is 2199999998
max_id   = 2199999999     (sanity: the range itself is intact)
{code}

{{lag(id, 1)}} over ids {{0..2199999999}} must yield {{NULL, 0, 1, ..., 2199999998}}, so
{{max(prev)}} must be {{2199999998}}; it returned NULL for every row.

For {{2^31 < N < 2^32}} the wrapped count is negative, routing to the "offset outside
partition -> default" branch (silent NULLs). An {{ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException}} is the sibling
symptom when the wrapped count/index lands at an out-of-bounds value (needs {{N}} past
{{2^32}}). Same root cause, two symptoms.

h2. Root cause

File {{sql/core/.../execution/ExternalAppendOnlyUnsafeRowArray.scala}}:
* {{private var numRows = 0}} -- 32-bit {{Int}}, incremented per row in {{add()}}.
* {{def length: Int = numRows}} -- returns the overflowed count.

File {{sql/core/.../execution/window/WindowFunctionFrame.scala}}:
* {{OffsetWindowFunctionFrameBase.inputIndex}} -- 32-bit {{Int}} cursor into the partition.
* The {{absOffset > rows.length}} / {{inputIndex < input.length}} comparisons are wrong once
  {{length}} is negative.

In addition, the window drivers ({{WindowEvaluatorFactory}} and
{{ArrowWindowPythonEvaluatorFactory}}) track the per-partition row index as a 32-bit {{Int}}
({{rowIndex}}), and the sliding/ranking/segment-tree frames track their window bounds as
{{Int}}, so those frame types also cannot handle partitions larger than {{Int.MaxValue}} rows.

h2. Impact

Window queries over a single partition larger than {{Int.MaxValue}} rows can return silently
incorrect results (most visibly, {{lag}}/{{lead}} returning NULL for every row), or throw an
{{ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException}}, depending on the exact partition size and frame type.

h2. Fix direction

* Widen the row counter ({{numRows}}/{{length}}) and the offset frame's cursor to {{Long}} so
  {{lag}}/{{lead}} (and the unbounded-offset {{nth_value}} frame) produce correct results for
  large partitions.
* For the remaining frame types, which still rely on 32-bit row indices/bounds, fail the query
  with a clear user-facing error instead of silently producing wrong results. Full {{Long}}
  propagation for those frames (frame-bound API, aggregate processor, and the core
  {{UnsafeExternalSorter}} start index) is a larger follow-up.

Related: SPARK-51757 (write/insertion-path overflow in the same area).

title: Inline With definitions in filters inferred by InferFiltersFromConstraints
Offset log format v2 does not preserve stateful shuffle partitions across query restarts
description:
# Description

Offset log format v2 does not persist the stateful shuffle partition count used by a streaming query.

Consequently, when a stateful query is restarted with a different value of spark.sql.shuffle.partitions, Spark uses the current session value instead of the partition count recorded by the original execution. This changes the state-store partitioning and can make the checkpoint unrecoverable.

This is independent of offline state repartitioning. A normal stop-and-restart reproduces it.

Offset log v1 persists:

spark.sql.shuffle.partitions =
spark.sql.streaming.internal.stateStore.partitions

through the rebindSQLConfsSessionToOffsetLog mapping. However, OffsetSeqMetadataV2.apply copies only relevantSQLConfs and omits this rebinding.

During restart, IncrementalExecution.numStateStores cannot find the persisted value and falls back to the current session’s spark.sql.shuffle.partitions.

# Reproduction

1. Enable offset log format v2.
2. Start a stateful streaming aggregation with spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=5.
3. Process and commit at least one batch.
4. Stop the query.
5. Set spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=10.
6. Restart the query from the same checkpoint and process another batch.

For example:

withSQLConf(
SQLConf.STREAMING_OFFSET_LOG_FORMAT_VERSION.key -> "2",
SQLConf.SHUFFLE_PARTITIONS.key -> "5")

{ // Start a stateful aggregation, process data, and stop it. }

withSQLConf(
SQLConf.STREAMING_OFFSET_LOG_FORMAT_VERSION.key -> "2",
SQLConf.SHUFFLE_PARTITIONS.key -> "10")

{ // Restart from the same checkpoint and process more data. }

# Actual behavior

Spark reports:

Conf 'spark.sql.streaming.internal.stateStore.partitions' was not found
in the offset log. Using existing session conf value '10'.

The restarted physical plan uses:

Exchange hashpartitioning(..., 10), REQUIRED_BY_STATEFUL_OPERATOR

It then attempts to load state partitions that were never created by the original five-partition execution and fails, for example:

CANNOT_LOAD_STATE_STORE.CANNOT_READ_DELTA_FILE_NOT_EXISTS
.../state/0/6/1.delta does not exist

# Expected behavior

The query should retain the original five state-store partitions and restart successfully, regardless of the current session value of spark.sql.shuffle.partitions.

# Scope and compatibility

Offset log format v2 is not the default in Spark 4.2.0; the default remains v1. Therefore, default v1 queries are not affected.

However, any query using or requiring offset log format v2 can produce a checkpoint that cannot be restarted safely when the session shuffle-partition configuration changes.

This is a regression in the offset-log v2 implementation introduced under SPARK-54583 and is separate from the state-repartition-specific failure tracked by SPARK-59662.

# Suggested resolution
 - Make v2 persist the same stateful shuffle-partition rebinding as v1.
 - Add a regression test covering a normal 5-partition → 10-partition session restart.
 - Define recovery behavior for existing v2 checkpoints that already lack the configuration. Fixing only future writes will not repair those checkpoints. Recovery may need to infer the partition count from committed operator/state metadata before falling back to
the current session configuration.

# Related issues
 - SPARK-54583
 - SPARK-59662

title: PySpark raises internal errors instead of intended messages due to undefined error conditions and mismatched message parameters
description:
Several PySpark call sites raise a PySparkException with an error condition that does not exist in python/pyspark/errors/error-conditions.json, or with messageParameters that do not match the condition's template. Constructing the exception itself fails, so the user gets an unrelated internal error instead of the intended message, often with a different exception type (e.g. ValueError instead of TypeError).

h3. Undefined error conditions (fails with "ValueError: Cannot find main error class ...")
* NOT_STR - DataStreamReader.changes() (pyspark/sql/streaming/readwriter.py). NOT_STR was consolidated into NOT_EXPECTED_TYPE by SPARK-56179 while this new usage was added concurrently.
* VARIANT_SIZE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED - pyspark/sql/variant_utils.py (3 places)
* INVALID_OPERATION_UUID_ID - pyspark/sql/connect/client/core.py
* UNSUPPORTED_FILTER - pyspark/sql/worker/data_source_pushdown_filters.py

h3. Mismatched message parameters (fails with "AssertionError: Undefined error message parameter ...")
* DATA_SOURCE_EXTRANEOUS_FILTERS - pyspark/sql/worker/data_source_pushdown_filters.py passes extra "input" and "extraneous" parameters
* NO_ACTIVE_SESSION - pyspark/sql/connect/dataframe.py passes an extra "operator" parameter

h3. Reproduction
{code:python}
>>> spark.readStream.changes(123)
ValueError: Cannot find main error class 'NOT_STR'
{code}
Expected: PySparkTypeError saying that `tableName` should be a str.

The existing test for DATA_SOURCE_EXTRANEOUS_FILTERS (test_python_datasource.py) does not catch this, because it only asserts that the condition name appears in the exception text, which is also true of the AssertionError.

The JVM side guards against this in SparkThrowableSuite, but PySpark has no equivalent check.

h3. Proposed fix
Fix each call site, and add a test that scans PySpark sources for errorClass literals and verifies that each one is defined and that its literal messageParameters keys match the template.

UNSUPPORTED_PIPELINES_DATASET_TYPE has the same kind of problem but is already tracked in SPARK-57965, so it is out of scope here.

title: StreamingShuffleWriter leaks in-flight off-heap buffer when write fails
description:
When StreamingShuffleWriter.write() fails partway through, the in-flight off-heap buffer can be left unreleased: either it is referenced only by a local variable, or the send completion callback that releases it never runs. In both cases task completion cleanup does not release it. By default these buffers have no cleaner, so GC does not reclaim them either.

This only leaves a lasting leak when the failure is a non-fatal exception: a fatal error such as OutOfDirectMemoryError makes the executor exit, which frees its memory anyway. With UnsafeRowSerializer these paths are not expected to throw a non-fatal exception in normal operation, so this is a defensive fix. If one did occur, the buffer would stay allocated until the executor restarts.

Failure scenarios:
# The serializer throws while writing a record.
# Closing the serialization stream fails before a buffer is sent.
# Allocating or encoding the outgoing network frame fails before it is handed to the client, so the send completion callback never runs.

Expected behavior: when write() fails, StreamingShuffleWriter should release the in-flight buffer and return its memory budget before rethrowing the exception.

Reproduction (tested on 5.0.0-SNAPSHOT, master at commit 44929778453): run a streaming shuffle write with a serializer that throws on a given record (scenario 1) or on stream close (scenario 2). After the task fails, the captured buffer still has refCnt 1 and one buffer's worth of memory budget is not returned. For scenario 3, send a DataMessage whose data buffer throws while being encoded: the send completion callback is never invoked, so the buffer and its memory budget are never returned. With the fix, the buffer is released and the budget is fully returned in all three cases. Unit tests reproducing all three scenarios are included in the PR.

title: Storage-partitioned join sorts partitions the wrong way for an ORDER BY over a join-key expression
Storage-partitioned join fails with INTERNAL_ERROR when a one-side shuffle's join key references two columns
description:
With {{spark.sql.sources.v2.bucketing.shuffle.enabled}} on, this fails at planning with an {{INTERNAL_ERROR}} from the {{assert(refs.size == 1)}} in {{KeyedShuffleSpec.keyPositions}}. {{b4(id)}} is partitioned by {{bucket(4, id)}}, and {{pbc(b, c)}} and {{qxy(x, y)}} are not partitioned:
{code:sql}
SELECT * FROM b4
JOIN pbc p ON b4.id = p.b + p.c
JOIN qxy q ON p.b = q.x AND p.c = q.y
{code}
The first join shuffles {{pbc}} onto {{bucket(4, b + c)}}, which {{KeyedShuffleSpec.createPartitioning}} builds from its join key. The second join builds a shuffle spec for that layout, and {{keyPositions}} asserts that each partition expression has exactly one reference. A bucketed third table fails the same way.

Found while reviewing SPARK-59887. It fails on master and with SPARK-59887 alike.

title: Kubernetes Operator always replaces CR status 3 times on reconciliation
description:
In StatusRecorder, there is a for-loop which hardens the status update in case of intermittent connectivity issues, but the for loop keeps running even if the update was successful.

A spec update between these updates would have then triggered a 409 error, and the previous (successful) status update would have then triggered a `StatusConflictException`:.

title: Shut down AWS SDK v1 STS clients after S3 delegation-token acquisition
description:
AbstractS3DelegationTokenProvider.obtainDelegationTokens() creates an AWS SDK v1 STS client on each invocation but never explicitly shuts it down.

Both the Hadoop and Presto S3 delegation-token providers inherit this behavior. Consequently, client resources can remain allocated beyond the acquisition operation, including after failures.

The SDK has a finalizer-based cleanup path, but relying on its timing causes unnecessary resource retention.

I discovered this independently while working on the DPAT delegation-token [https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/spaces/FLINK/pages/430408507/FLIP-588+Support+per-job+delegation+tokens]. PR #27026 also addresses STS cleanup as part of a broader Hadoop/AWS SDK migration. This issue isolates the cleanup fix for the existing SDK v1 implementation so it can be reviewed and considered for backporting independently of that migration.

title: Fix wrong results when a storage-partitioned join pairs a transform of a join-key expression with one of a column
description:
With {{spark.sql.sources.v2.bucketing.shuffle.enabled}} on, a storage-partitioned join can return wrong results when a side that was shuffled onto a transform of a join-key expression meets another bucketed table in a later join.

Repro, with AQE and broadcast joins off. {{t1(id bigint)}} and {{t3(x bigint)}} are partitioned by {{bucket(4, ...)}}, {{plain(b bigint)}} is not partitioned, and each holds the values 0 to 7:
{code:sql}
SELECT t1.id, p.b, t3.x FROM t1
JOIN plain p ON t1.id = p.b + 1
JOIN t3 ON p.b = t3.x
{code}
The query should return 7 rows. It returns 0, and the second join has no shuffle.

Why:
* The first join shuffles {{plain}} onto {{t1}}'s partitioning. {{KeyedShuffleSpec.createPartitioning}} builds that partitioning from {{plain}}'s join key, so it is {{bucket(4, b + 1)}}.
* The second join clusters {{plain}} on the bare {{b}}. {{KeyedShuffleSpec.keyPositions}} maps a partition expression to a cluster key by its reference, so {{bucket(4, b + 1)}} counts as a function of {{b}}, the counterpart of {{x}}.
* {{TransformExpression.isSameFunction}} compares only the function name and the bucket count, so {{bucket(4, b + 1)}} is the same as {{t3}}'s {{bucket(4, x)}}, and the join pairs the partitions as they stand. A row with {{b = x}} sits in bucket {{(b + 1) % 4}} on one side and in {{x % 4}} on the other.

Measured on master. The one-side shuffle of transform expressions came with SPARK-48012 (4.0.0).

title: PARSE_JSON fails with NullPointerException when allowDuplicateKeys is NULL
Fluss sink rejects pre-created primary-key tables with custom bucket keys
description:
h2. Description

The Fluss sink rejects a pre-created table when its bucket keys differ from the default inferred from the primary key, even when the source and sink tables have identical definitions.

h2. Steps to reproduce

# Pre-create identical Fluss source and sink tables with:
## Columns: \{{id INT NOT NULL, tenant INT NOT NULL, marker STRING}}
## Primary key: \{{(id, tenant)}}
## Bucket keys: \{{(tenant, id)}}
## Bucket count: \{{2}}
# Start a Fluss-to-Fluss CDC pipeline without sink \{{bucket.key}} or \{{bucket.num}} overrides.

The initial \{{CreateTableEvent}} fails with:

{code}
ValidationException:
New Fluss table's bucket keys : [id, tenant]
Current Fluss's bucket keys: [tenant, id]
{code}

The same problem occurs when both tables use a valid bucket-key subset, such as \{{(tenant)}}.

h2. Root cause

{\{FlussConversions.toFlussTable()}} defaults unspecified bucket keys to primary keys minus partition keys. \{{FlussMetaDataApplier.sanityCheck()}} then compares this inferred list with the existing table's bucket keys using \{{List.equals}}, treating a table-creation default as an existing-table constraint.

h2. Expected behavior and proposed fix

Accept the compatible pre-created table and preserve its layout.

For existing primary-key tables without an explicit bucket-key override, accept target bucket keys that are a subset of the inferred keys, regardless of order. Preserve strict ordered comparison for explicit overrides and leave new-table creation unchanged.

Both cases were reproduced through \{{FlussMetadataApplierTest}} on \{{3.7-SNAPSHOT}}.

title: KafkaDynamicSink#equals/hashCode ignore transactionNamingStrategy
description:
KafkaDynamicSink.equals() and .hashCode() do not include the field transactionNamingStrategy.

The field, together with the table option sink.transaction-naming-strategy, was introduced before. That change added the field to the constructor, to copy() and to the KafkaSinkBuilder call, but not to equals/hashCode, which still compare every other configuration field of the sink (delivery guarantee, transactional id prefix, topics, partitioner, flush mode, parallelism, ...).

KafkaDynamicSource compares all of its configuration fields.

Impact:
 * Two KafkaDynamicSink instances that differ only in the naming strategy (INCREMENTING vs POOLING) compare equal.
 * KafkaDynamicTableFactoryTest#testTableSinkStrategyTranslation and UpsertKafkaDynamicTableFactoryTest#testTableSinkStrategyTranslation assert actualSink.isEqualTo(expectedSink). Because equals ignores the strategy, these tests pass for any value, so a regression in the option translation (e.g. the factory passing TransactionNamingStrategy.DEFAULT instead of the configured value) would not be detected.
 * No runtime impact: the planner does not compare DynamicTableSink instances, and the runtime sink is built from the field directly in getSinkRuntimeProvider. The sink is @Internal.

 

Fix: add transactionNamingStrategy to equals and hashCode. Optionally strengthen the two translation tests by asserting that the actual sink is not equal to an expected sink built with a different strategy, which fails without the fix and passes with it.

title: ASOF JOIN matches NULL STRUCT operands because MATCH_CONDITION rebuilds them from their fields
description:
In SQL ASOF JOIN, a NULL STRUCT operand can match, but a NULL must never match.
{code:sql}
  SET spark.sql.join.asofJoin.enabled=true;
  SELECT r.tag
  FROM VALUES (CAST(NULL AS STRUCT<a: INT>), 'l') AS t(k, tag)
  ASOF JOIN VALUES (CAST(NULL AS STRUCT<a: INT>), 'rnull'), (named_struct('a', 1), 'r1') AS r(k, tag)
    MATCH_CONDITION (t.k >= r.k);
  {code}
Expected: no row. Actual: rnull.

Cause: before comparing, ASOF rebuilds each struct from its fields. A NULL struct becomes a struct with a NULL field, which is
not NULL, so it matches. A plain WHERE with the same comparison is correct.

This happens for flat and nested structs, with ANSI on and off.

Fix: keep a NULL struct NULL when ASOF rebuilds it.

Assigned to: [~lukazdravic] 

Umbrella: SPARK-59526

title: Fix deadlock in StreamingQueryListenerBus when removing the last listener
Register an accumulator with the TaskContext only after it is fully deserialized
description:
{{AccumulatorV2.readObject}} registers the accumulator with the {{{}TaskContext{}}}, which publishes it where other threads can reach it. That runs at {{{}AccumulatorV2{}}}'s own slot during deserialization, and Java serialization reads class data superclass-first, so no subclass field has been assigned yet.

A subclass holding its state in a {{val}} therefore exposes a null for that window. The reader that hits it in practice is the executor heartbeater, which calls {{isZero}} on every registered accumulator every {{{}spark.executor.heartbeatInterval{}}}. The NPE is thrown on the {{executor-heartbeater}} thread and propagates out of a {{scheduleAtFixedRate}} task, so the executor stops heartbeating permanently; the driver then removes it on heartbeat timeout, losing anything held only there — e.g. local checkpoint blocks, which surfaces as {{{}CHECKPOINT_RDD_BLOCK_ID_NOT_FOUND{}}}.

Because a Scala {{val}} compiles to a final field, there is a second aspect: the reflective write happens after publication, so per JLS 17.5.3 a reader has no guarantee of ever seeing it and the JIT may fold the read.

SPARK-20977 fixed this locally in {{CollectionAccumulator}} by making its state a non-final field reached through a lazily-initializing accessor. Every subclass since has had to re-derive that workaround, and not all have: {{SetAccumulator}} in {{sql/execution/debug}} still dereferences a {{private val _set}} from {{{}isZero{}}}, and {{EventTimeStatsAccum}} avoids the NPE only incidentally, because Scala's {{==}} is null-safe — it reports the wrong answer and ships a null instead.

Fix: register in {{{}readResolve{}}}, which Java serialization invokes only after every class in the hierarchy has been read. The accumulator is then never observable half-initialized and no subclass needs to guard its own state.

Verified with a new test using a subclass that holds state in a plain {{val}} with no null handling: it fails with the NPE on current {{master}} and passes with registration moved, while the existing {{{}LongAccumulator{}}}/{{{}DoubleAccumulator{}}}/{{{}CollectionAccumulator{}}} tests are unaffected.

title: Align table and changelog state-option handling and metadata reuse
description:
{{TableCatalog.tableStateOptionKeys()}} was introduced in Spark 4.3.0 by [PR #57799|https://github.com/apache/spark/pull/57799] ([commit 4b4a2f7b69d5|https://github.com/apache/spark/commit/4b4a2f7b69d555a2b28a130092f7d75411cb4c49]). That change made ordinary table loading and metadata reuse honor declared table-state options, while {{loadChangelog}} retained its all-options contract.

TableCatalog currently has different option-handling contracts for ordinary table reads and changelog reads:

* {{tableStateOptionKeys()}} declares the connector options that select table state. Spark passes only those options to {{loadTable(Identifier, TableContext, stateOptions)}} and uses them for table metadata reuse. Complete per-read options remain available for scan planning.
* {{loadChangelog(Identifier, ChangelogContext, options)}} receives all query options, and changelog resolution bypasses the corresponding state-aware table-loading/cache path. There is no separate changelog state-option declaration.

State options do reach CDC connectors, but Spark does not apply the same option projection and metadata-reuse rules to the two paths. This complicates deduplicating loads and refreshes, including the ongoing work on concurrent table refresh.

For example, a current-table read and a changes-from-version-1 read with matching table-state options should be able to share the underlying captured table state. Their scan options and changelog range still describe distinct reads. Different state options must remain isolated, and different changelog contexts must not be treated as equivalent reads.

The goal is to define consistent state-option, caching, and refresh semantics for ordinary and changelog reads, while retaining complete scan options and preserving the requested CDC context through refresh.

The API approach is undecided. This ticket does not prescribe changing the Changelog hierarchy, adding a baseTable accessor, or any particular wrapper or refresh-request abstraction. The implementation should be evaluated for compatibility with existing connector APIs for the Spark 4.3.0 release.

References:
* [TableCatalog option contracts|https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/29acd89ec5f4806c1f6a335d8d3136baf111cd08/sql/catalyst/src/main/java/org/apache/spark/sql/connector/catalog/TableCatalog.java#L104]
* [Current changelog resolution|https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/29acd89ec5f4806c1f6a335d8d3136baf111cd08/sql/catalyst/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/sql/catalyst/analysis/RelationResolution.scala#L382]
* [Exploratory prototype for discussion; API not decided|https://github.com/gengliangwang/spark/pull/20]

Target release: Spark 4.3.0.

title: INSERT with a column list fails when an omitted column is of type VARIANT
description:
An INSERT with an explicit column list fails during validation when the target table has a VARIANT column that is not listed.
{code:sql}
CREATE TABLE src (k INT) WITH ('connector' = 'datagen', 'number-of-rows' = '1');
CREATE TABLE snk (k INT, v VARIANT) WITH ('connector' = 'blackhole');

INSERT INTO snk SELECT k, CAST(NULL AS VARIANT) FROM src;  -- works
INSERT INTO snk (k) SELECT k FROM src;                     -- fails
{code}
{noformat}
org.apache.flink.table.api.ValidationException: SQL validation failed. Unsupported type when convertTypeToSpec: VARIANT
Caused by: java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException: Unsupported type when convertTypeToSpec: VARIANT
    at org.apache.calcite.sql.type.SqlTypeUtil.convertTypeToSpec(SqlTypeUtil.java:1326)
    at org.apache.calcite.sql.validate.SqlValidatorImpl.maybeCast(SqlValidatorImpl.java:819)
    at org.apache.flink.table.planner.calcite.FlinkCalciteSqlValidator.maybeCast(FlinkCalciteSqlValidator.java:491)
    at org.apache.flink.table.planner.calcite.PreValidateReWriter$.appendPartitionAndNullsProjects(PreValidateReWriter.scala:187)
{noformat}
Nested types fail too, for example {{{}ARRAY<VARIANT>{}}}, {{ROW<f VARIANT>}} and {{{}MAP<STRING, VARIANT>{}}}.

*Cause*

{{PreValidateReWriter}} pads every omitted column with {{{}CAST(NULL AS <column type>){}}}. The cast target is built by {{{}SqlTypeUtil.convertTypeToSpec{}}}. VARIANT is not covered by {{{}SqlTypeUtil.isAtomic{}}}, so no branch matches. Calcite fixed this in CALCITE-7293, which ships with Calcite 1.42.0. Flink is on 1.41.0.

*Proposed fix*

Backport CALCITE-7293 to Flink's copy of {{SqlTypeUtil}} by adding VARIANT to {{{}isAtomic{}}}. The backport can be dropped once FLINK-40001 upgrades to Calcite 1.42.0.

Flink disables Calcite's implicit type coercion, so the {{isAtomic}} change has no effect outside {{{}convertTypeToSpec{}}}.

BITMAP, RAW and STRUCTURED columns fail the same way. They are Flink types that Calcite does not know, so they are fixed separately in FLINK-40840

The workaround is to list every column and write {{CAST(NULL AS VARIANT)}} for the omitted ones.

{{CAST(NULL AS VARIANT)}} will work once FLINK-40825 is resolved

title: Validate bounds in the vectorized BYTE_STREAM_SPLIT reader
description:
Follow-up of SPARK-59812. The vectorized BYTE_STREAM_SPLIT reader (VectorizedByteStreamSplitValuesReader, added by SPARK-56894) does not validate its position against the page, so a corrupt page can be decoded silently:

* The skip methods (skipIntegers, skipLongs, skipFloats, skipDoubles, skipBytes, skipShorts, skipBinary, skipFixedLenByteArray) only do `offset += total`, without checking that the page has that many values. The read paths index pageData without a bound check either, so reading past the end reads bytes from the next stream or fails with an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of a ParquetDecodingException.
* initFromPage derives the value count as `totalBytes / typeWidth` and does not reject `totalBytes % typeWidth != 0`. For such a page, every stream starts at the wrong offset, so every value is silently decoded from the wrong bytes.

SPARK-56894 is in branch-4.3 and v4.3.0-rc1, so this should be fixed before 4.3.0 is released.

title: Fix overflow in forward ASOF join by keeping the first match
ExecutionMemoryPool.acquireMemory throws NoSuchElementException when the task's entry is removed while it waits
description:
ExecutionMemoryPool.acquireMemory registers the task's memoryForTask entry once, before its wait loop, and reads the entry with memoryForTask(taskAttemptId) on every pass of the loop. releaseMemory removes the entry when the task's balance reaches zero and calls notifyAll. A caller that was parked in lock.wait() and wakes after that removal throws java.util.NoSuchElementException: key not found: <taskAttemptId> instead of continuing to wait or being granted memory.

On master (core/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/memory/ExecutionMemoryPool.scala):

* lines 103-104: the entry is registered only if absent, before the loop
* line 115: val curMem = memoryForTask(taskAttemptId), no default
* line 142: lock.wait()
* lines 165-167: releaseMemory subtracts and removes the entry at zero

The entry can be removed under a waiting caller because TaskMemoryManager.releaseExecutionMemory does not take the TaskMemoryManager monitor that acquireExecutionMemory holds while it waits. Any consumer of the same task that releases through releaseExecutionMemory (MemoryConsumer.freeMemory, or a caller on another thread) can bring the balance to zero while another acquire of that task is parked below its share.

Reproduction (component level, off-heap UnifiedMemoryManager with 100 bytes, storageFraction 0):

# Task 0 acquires 10 bytes. Task 1 acquires 90 bytes.
# On another thread, task 0 calls acquireExecutionMemory(20). It parks, because 10 is below the minimum share of 25 for two active tasks.
# Task 0's consumer frees its 10 bytes with freeMemory. The balance is zero, so releaseMemory removes the entry and wakes the waiter.
# The waiter throws NoSuchElementException: key not found: 0.

Expected: the parked acquire keeps waiting, or is granted, exactly as if the entry had stayed. The caller has nothing from the failed call, so there is no accounting to undo, but the exception is not a memory error and callers such as UnsafeExternalSorter do not treat it as a signal to spill.

Suggested fix: read the entry with memoryForTask.getOrElseUpdate(taskAttemptId, 0L) inside the loop (or re-register after waking), so a removed entry is recreated at zero and the loop continues.

Seen in Apache DataFusion Comet, whose native memory consumer parks in this loop while other consumers of the task release: https://github.com/apache/datafusion-comet/issues/6224 and https://github.com/apache/datafusion-comet/issues/6304. Comet works around it by retrying the acquire.

title: VariantBuilder.of(BigDecimal) writes malformed or wrong decimals for negative scale or precision/scale > 38
description:
h3. Problem

{{BinaryVariantInternalBuilder.appendDecimal(BigDecimal)}} writes {{(byte) d.scale()}} without validating the decimal. There is no check for a negative scale at all. Precision and scale above 38 are only guarded by a Java {{assert}} in the DECIMAL16 branch, which only runs with {{-ea}} and is off by default. The [Parquet variant spec|https://parquet.apache.org/docs/file-format/types/variantencoding/] requires a scale in [0, 38] and a precision of at most 38 for decimal4/8/16.

This can be reached through the public {{{}VariantBuilder.of(BigDecimal){}}}, e.g. from a UDF that returns a variant:
{code:java}
Variant v = Variant.newBuilder().of(new BigDecimal("1e5")); // scale -5
v.getType();    // DECIMAL
v.getDecimal(); // VariantTypeException: MALFORMED_VARIANT
v.toJson();     // VariantTypeException: MALFORMED_VARIANT

// 41 digits: same as above without -ea, AssertionError with -ea
Variant.newBuilder().of(new BigDecimal("1" + "0".repeat(40)));

// the scale byte wraps, so this silently reads back as 0.1
Variant.newBuilder().of(new BigDecimal("1e2147483647")).toString();
{code}
The reader ({{{}BinaryVariantUtil.getDecimalWithOriginalScale{}}}) checks the range, so a broken value is written without error and only fails later when it's read. In the wrap-around case it doesn't fail at all and returns a wrong value.

A negative scale is easy to get: {{Variant.getDecimal()}} strips trailing zeros, so a variant holding 100 returns {{{}1E+2{}}}. Passing that back to {{of(BigDecimal)}} gives a malformed variant.

PARSE_JSON is not affected. {{tryParseDecimal}} only accepts plain decimals without an exponent and checks the range before calling {{{}appendDecimal{}}}. Otherwise it falls back to double.
h3. How Spark handles it

Our builder is a port of Spark's {{{}VariantBuilder{}}}, and Spark's {{appendDecimal}} has the same code: no negative scale check and the same {{{}assert{}}}. Spark relies on the callers instead:
 * {{parse_json}} uses the same {{tryParseDecimal}} check as we do.
 * {{CAST(... AS VARIANT)}} relies on {{DecimalType}} (precision <= 38, scale >= 0 unless the legacy negative scale flag is enabled).
 * The CSV and XML parsers reject a scale below -38, rescale a negative scale with {{{}setScale(0){}}}, and then require precision and scale <= 38 (SPARK-54099, SPARK-55932).

We can't rely on the callers in the same way because {{VariantBuilder.of(BigDecimal)}} is public API and accepts any BigDecimal.
h3. Proposed fix

Validate in {{appendDecimal}} with the same rules as Spark's CSV/XML parsers:
 * Rescale a negative scale to 0 with {{{}setScale(0){}}}. This keeps the value. Non-zero values with a scale below -38 are rejected first. They can't fit anyway, and {{setScale}} is expensive for huge exponents like {{{}1e999999999{}}}.
 * Throw a {{VariantTypeException}} if the precision or scale is still above 38.

title: Validate value lengths and skip amounts in the vectorized PLAIN, DELTA_LENGTH_BYTE_ARRAY and DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY readers
description:
Similar to SPARK-59352, the vectorized PLAIN and DELTA_LENGTH_BYTE_ARRAY readers use value lengths and skip amounts that come from the file without validating them. The read paths mostly fail on a corrupt page, but the skip paths (used when column-index filtering produces row ranges) do not:

* VectorizedDeltaLengthByteArrayReader.skipBinary loops on `remaining -= in.skip(remaining)`. When a length runs past the end of the page, ByteBufferInputStream.skip returns -1, so `remaining` grows until the int overflows (~2^31 iterations per value), then the read silently continues. A negative length is silently skipped.
* VectorizedPlainValuesReader.skipBinary calls `in.skip(len)` on a length read from the file. With SingleBufferInputStream a negative length moves the stream position backwards, so later values in the page are decoded from the wrong offset and the query returns wrong results without an error. A too-short skip is silently ignored.
* The fixed-width skips in VectorizedPlainValuesReader (skipIntegers, skipLongs, skipFloats, skipDoubles, skipBytes, skipShorts, skipFixedLenByteArray) ignore the return value of `in.skip`.
* On the read paths, a negative length is not rejected either: slicing a negative length also moves the position backwards, or fails with an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of a ParquetDecodingException.

Note that ByteBufferInputStream.skipFully does not reject a negative length on SingleBufferInputStream, so negative lengths need an explicit check.

The fix rejects negative lengths on both the read and skip paths, and makes the skip paths fail with a ParquetDecodingException when the page does not have enough bytes, matching the read paths.

title: Remove JIRA fix versions when merging reverts
description:
The merge script recognizes revert PR titles but still routes their JIRA updates through the resolve/add flow. Fix versions can therefore remain on a ticket after the associated change has been reverted.

Spark release issue lists use JIRA fix versions. These stale entries can cause release notes to list changes absent from the release and require manual cleanup by release managers.

When merging or backporting a revert, offer to remove recorded, unreleased fix versions inferred from the branches receiving the revert. Allow the committer to edit, skip, and confirm the selection, preserve other versions and ticket status, and support dry runs.

title: Fix UTF-8 byte limits and physical line numbers during event log replay
description:
SPARK-59407 (commit 38258cbea90) introduced bounded event-log line reading in ReplayListenerBus. There are two related correctness issues:

1. spark.history.fs.eventLog.maxLineLength is a byte-valued configuration, but boundedLines compares StringBuilder.length() * 2 with the configured limit. This measures UTF-16 storage rather than UTF-8 input length. With an 8 KiB limit, a valid ASCII SparkListenerApplicationStart event containing a 6,000-character application name (approximately 6 KiB of JSON) is incorrectly skipped. Multibyte UTF-8 input also has inconsistent boundaries. A trailing CR in CRLF is counted before being removed.

2. boundedLines removes oversized lines before replay applies zipWithIndex. Consequently, subsequent parse diagnostics report renumbered positions instead of physical file lines. For example, a valid event on line 1, oversized lines 2 and 3, and an invalid event {} on line 4 produce "Malformed line #2" instead of "Malformed line #4".

The proposed fix counts UTF-8 content bytes, excludes line endings from the limit, and carries original line indices through skipped lines. It preserves strict rejection of malformed UTF-8, filtered iterator behavior, and truncated-log handling. Buffer growth remains bounded by the configured line limit; the limit specifies encoded content length rather than an exact JVM heap budget.

Local regression coverage includes ASCII content, 1- through 4-byte UTF-8 characters, exact and over-limit boundaries, decoder-buffer crossings, LF/CRLF/unterminated final lines, physical line numbers after multiple skipped lines, filtered iterators, truncated logs, and malformed UTF-8 in oversized lines.

Validation: the original implementation fails three new regression tests. With the fix, all 11 tests in ReplayListenerSuite pass under SBT, and both production and test scalastyle checks pass.

title: Fix internal error for non-foldable options maps

title: Initialize the global aggregation once per empty batch in the streamline plan
description:
A global streaming aggregation on the streamline (Real-Time Mode) plan drops the initialized result for an executed empty batch:

* a source batch whose RDD has no partitions: the buffer is never initialized, no state is created, and no row is emitted;
* a batch with multiple empty partitions: one seeded row per empty partition (duplicate rows);
* a non-empty batch that has an empty sibling partition: an extra seeded row.

The ordinary micro-batch plan initializes the global buffer exactly once and emits the initialized result (count 0, sum NULL) for an executed empty batch, so the streamline plan diverges from it.

Fix: plan the non-final ProjectAggregationBufferExec with a single-partition (AllTuples) requirement for a global aggregation, so its empty-input guard fires exactly once per executed empty batch and never for a batch that has input. The projection propagates the single partition, so the plan keeps exactly one exchange; grouped aggregations are unchanged.

Follow-up to SPARK-58635.

title: Source-topic changelog store gets the task's last produced offset instead of its last consumed offset when the task writes to its own source topic
description: When a KTable uses its source topic as its changelog (topology.optimization=all or reuse.ktable.source.topics, or Topology#addReadOnlyStateStore) and the same task also writes to that source topic, StreamTask#checkpointableOffsets() gives the offset the task produced precedence over the offset it consumed:

title: Clear next offsets to consume on task close to avoid stale commit after revive
description:
A revived active task (`closeDirtyAndRevive`) kept `nextOffsetsAndMetadataToBeConsumed`
from before the corruption. After the consumer is seeked back to its committed offset, a
commit driven by processor metadata (`needsCommit`, which commits all input partitions)
could fall back to that stale next offset and commit past records the task hasn't
reprocessed — skipping them if the task later moves, and purging them for a repartition
topic. The KAFKA-20416 `consumedOffsets.clear()` fix does not cover this path.

Fix: clear `nextOffsetsAndMetadataToBeConsumed` in `StreamTask.close()`, alongside
`consumedOffsets`, so a revived task has no stale fallback for a partition it hasn't
re-read.

title: State processor API no longer rejects key types that cannot be hashed reliably
description:
FLINK-40751 replaced `stream.keyBy(keySelector)` in `StateBootstrapTransformation` with a `PartitionTransformation` built directly, so the key type validation that `KeyedStream` performs is no longer reached. `OneInputStateTransformation#keyBy` only extracts the key type, so nothing validates it now.

Before, bootstrapping keyed state with an array key failed at build time:

{code}
InvalidProgramException: Type byte[] cannot be used as key. Contained UNSUPPORTED key types: byte[]. Look at the keyBy() documentation for the conditions a type has to satisfy in order to be eligible for a key.
{code}

On master the same job builds, runs and writes a savepoint. The same applies to an enum key and to a POJO that does not override `hashCode`.

The check comes from FLINK-5874, which restricted key types in the DataStream API because such a key cannot be hashed reliably. Without it the state is not partitioned consistently: two equal `byte[] {1, 2, 3}` keys can be assigned to different key groups (48 and 39 in a local run with `maxParallelism` 128). A job restoring the savepoint would reject the key type in its own `keyBy`, so the effect is that an up-front error is replaced by a savepoint that cannot be used.

Reported by Gyula Fora on https://github.com/apache/flink/pull/29268 as worth fixing with a test.

title: CAST in Table API ignores input nullability when the target type is NOT NULL
description:
In the Table API, a CAST to a target written with .notNull() is planned as NOT NULL even when the input may be null. The CAST type strategy already derives the result as nullable, but CastConverter builds the RexNode from the literal target type. The optimizer trusts the wrong NOT NULL and can fold null checks away, which drops rows or produces wrong values.

h3. Reproduce

{code:java}
Table t = tEnv.fromValues(
        ROW(FIELD("i", INT())),
        Row.of((Object) null),
        Row.of(1));

t.select($("i").cast(BIGINT().notNull()).as("c"))
        .filter($("c").isNull())
        .execute()
        .print();
{code}

Expected: one row with c = NULL.
Actual: empty result. The plan collapses to an empty Values because IS NULL is folded to FALSE.

The same happens for a nested VARIANT input, e.g. parseJson(s).cast(ARRAY(VARIANT())).cast(ARRAY(INT()).notNull()). FLINK-40672 only covered a top-level VARIANT input.

SQL is not affected. A SQL CAST cannot declare NOT NULL on the target, and SqlCastFunction.deriveType takes the nullability from the input.

h3. Proposed fix

CastConverter should use the resolved output type of the call, which the type strategy derives from the input, instead of the literal target type. This aligns the Table API with SQL for all casts. As a side effect, casting a NOT NULL input to a nullable target now yields NOT NULL, as it already does in SQL.

Also document on cast() that the top-level nullability of the target type is ignored.
